query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, degradation of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy is governed by the formation of a heterogeneous oxide scale that preferentially forms at grain boundaries. This scale—originating from the selective oxidation of the more reactive elements (e.g., Ti and Cr) in the fine-grained FCC matrix—reduces the cohesive strength of the grain boundaries and acts as a stress concentrator. When exposed to strongly oxidizing environments, the thicker and less adherent oxide scale leads to accelerated grain boundary decohesion and catastrophic intergranular failure, while reducing environments may delay or modify the oxidation process and resulting degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy in a predominantly FCC solid solution—likely exhibiting a fine microstructure with residual internal stresses from rapid solidification.
generation.intervention: Control the gas atmosphere during high‐temperature exposure by varying the oxygen partial pressure to create strongly oxidizing versus reducing environments.
generation.conditions: Expose samples at an elevated temperature (e.g., ≥700 °C) for a fixed duration under two controlled atmospheres: one with high oxygen partial pressure (oxidizing) and one with low oxygen activity or the presence of a reducing gas. All other parameters, such as temperature and exposure time, are kept constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of an oxide scale and its localization along the grain boundaries (and possibly at processing-induced defects) that undermines intergranular cohesion.
generation.mechanism: At high temperature, oxygen diffuses along grain boundaries and preferentially oxidizes reactive species (notably Ti and Cr), forming a layered, heterogeneous oxide. This oxide scale is poorly adherent and grows primarily along the grain boundaries, weakening the bonding between grains. The weakened, oxidized boundaries become sites for stress concentration and crack initiation, leading to catastrophic intergranular failure, especially under oxidizing conditions. In contrast, a reducing atmosphere suppresses extensive oxide growth, thereby mitigating the degradation process.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-manufactured state (baseline under moderate oxygen activity), samples exposed to strongly oxidizing conditions will develop a thicker, discontinuous oxide scale along grain boundaries, leading to marked grain boundary embrittlement and an increased incidence of catastrophic failure (e.g., intergranular fracture). Under reducing conditions, the oxide scale will be thinner or less pervasive, resulting in less degradation of mechanical integrity.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured alloy exposed to standard testing conditions with moderate oxygen partial pressure.
generation.boundary: Exposure conditions at elevated temperature (≥700 °C) and gas atmospheres where oxygen activity is either well above (oxidizing) or below (reducing) a controlled threshold that influences oxide formation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative differences in oxide scale thickness, the critical oxygen partial pressure that triggers catastrophic failure, and potential interactions with residual stresses from the additive manufacturing process remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of identical additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy samples and subject them to high-temperature exposure (e.g., ≥700 °C for a fixed time) under two different atmospheres: a strongly oxidizing environment (high oxygen partial pressure) and a reducing environment (low oxygen activity or with a reducing gas). After exposure, characterize the oxide layer thickness and distribution along grain boundaries using high-resolution SEM/TEM and assess mechanical properties (e.g., tensile or creep testing) to determine the mode and temperature of failure.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity (via TEM/SEM imaging)
Elemental distribution at grain boundaries (via EDS or XPS)
Mechanical property degradation (tensile strength, ductility, or creep life)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under strongly oxidizing conditions, the oxide scale formation and associated intergranular weakening are not significantly different from those observed under reducing conditions (or compared to the baseline), and if there is no corresponding increase in catastrophic failure (e.g., intergranular fracture), then the mechanism that attributes degradation to grain boundary-specific oxidation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Al seems to have a minor effect on both Ni and Co, both of which are the weakest oxidizing component and it seems to have no effects on both unoxidized and oxidized states. We infer that Al addition does not have significant electronic interaction with Co and Ni (Fig. 4h, i), this is shown as their oxidation behavior remains the same in Fig. 4d. Figure 4j summarizes these interactions where Mn-Al tends to have the strongest interaction and both Ni and Co being the weakest. This study uncovers the oxidation process in compositionally complex alloys. Our study involved subjecting an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy to oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar oxygen pressure for both ex situ and in situ observations. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide). We chose a relatively low oxidation temperature to prevent phase transformation in the alloy, focusing solely on examining the oxidation process in the super-saturated alloy condition.
